title: attention-kernel-profiling-flash-paged-fused-2026-03
content:
Executive summary:

This working note collects profiling results and observations from our recent experiments comparing FlashAttention, paged (KV paging) attention, and fused attention kernels (fused qkv + attention + output projection). Tests were run on representative decoder-only models and serve-stack harnesses to identify practical bottlenecks for production inference at scale.

Key takeaways:
- FlashAttention yields substantial GPU compute savings for medium-to-long sequences (512+), but orchestration and memory-copy overheads reduce wall-clock wins for short sequences (<=128) in our runtime.
- Paged attention (KV paging) dramatically reduces peak GPU memory footprint for long-context workloads (4k+), enabling larger batch sizes on A100 80GB, but incurs additional kernel launch overhead and CPU/GPU synchronization that increases tail latency if not carefully overlapped.
- Fused kernels (qkv matmul + bias + rotary + softmax fused) reduce kernel launch count and intermediate memory writes, providing the best tail-latency improvement in our continuous-batching setup. The combination of FlashAttention with operator fusion gives the most consistent latency/throughput profile.

Experiment setup:
- Models: small decoder-only toy model (350M), production-like 7B transformer (decoder-only), and a trimmed 33B profile run to check scaling behavior.
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB (primary), spot checks on H100 SXM.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime (local branch: profiler/attention-2026) with continuous batching enabled.
- Frameworks/kernels tested: xformers/FlashAttention v2, in-house paged-KV implementation (paged-kv-v3), fused-ops from our compiler branch (fusion/ops-fused-2026).
- Sequences: 64, 128, 512, 2048, 4096 (where applicable).
- Batch sizes: Single-request (batch=1) and high-concurrency (batch=8 aggregated by runtime).
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p99 per-token latency, end-to-end latency, GPU utilization (SM), GPU memory peaks, kernel launch counts, PCIe copy times, CPU-side scheduling stall time.

Profiling highlights and raw observations:
1) Short sequences (<=128) — latency-sensitive paths
- FlashAttention compute is efficient but the runtime spends 30-40% of time outside CUDA kernels (scheduling, memcpy, and queue drains) for batch=1. Observed p90 token latency improvement vs baseline attention: ~8-12% on A100; p99 improvement smaller (~5%).
- Fused kernels reduce number of kernel launches by ~3-4 per attention op. This decreased p99 latency by ~15% relative to baseline on short sequences because launch overheads are a larger fraction of total time.
- Paged KV shows no benefit here and often regresses latency due to extra orchestration.

2) Medium sequences (512) — compute-dominated but still latency-sensitive
- FlashAttention shows 20-35% throughput improvement and ~18% p50 per-token latency reduction for 7B model on A100 vs naive attention (softmax + batched GEMMs + transpose).
- The best results came from combining FlashAttention with fused upstream ops (qkv fusion) — extra ~8-10% improvement. This indicates that overlapping fewer kernels matters as much as algorithmic savings.
- GPU utilization (SM%) increased from ~62% (baseline) to ~80% (Flash + fusion).

3) Long sequences (2k-4k) — memory and KV management bottlenecks
- Paged KV reduced peak GPU memory by up to 45% for 4k contexts enabling batch sizes 2-3x larger on A100 80GB. This directly improved throughput for long-context use cases where baseline O(L^2) memory killed batch scaling.
- However, paged KV increases CPU->GPU synchronization events several times; unless the runtime overlaps paging with other compute/requests, p99 latency can increase by 1.2-1.5x.
- FlashAttention remains beneficial when combined with intelligent KV placement (keep active KV in GPU, page cold KV to host). The hybrid approach (paged storage + FlashAttention compute) provides best tradeoff.

Bottleneck breakdown (most impactful items observed):
- Kernel launch overheads and small-kernel inefficiency (dominant for short sequences).
- PCIe/host-device memcpy stalls when KV paging is enabled and not overlapped.
- Transpose/permute intermediate buffers (mem-bound) when fusion is not applied.
- Softmax numerical stability variants that add extra kernels (e.g., row-wise max/subtract then exponent) — FlashAttention's fused softmax improves both perf and numerical stability in our tests.
- CPU-side scheduling contention in the serving runtime when concurrent requests arrive with different seq lengths — leads to queuing and tail latency spikes.

Representative numbers (7B model, A100, single-request latency and tokens/s):
- Baseline (naive attention): seq=512 p50 token-latency = 2.8 ms, p99 = 7.2 ms, throughput ~ 75k tokens/s
- FlashAttention only: seq=512 p50 = 2.3 ms, p99 = 6.0 ms, throughput ~ 95k tokens/s
- Fused ops only: seq=512 p50 = 2.1 ms, p99 = 5.8 ms, throughput ~ 102k tokens/s
- Flash + fused: seq=512 p50 = 1.9 ms, p99 = 4.9 ms, throughput ~ 118k tokens/s
(These numbers are illustrative and reflect our measurement noise; exact values depend on micro-batching and continuous-batching policies.)

Implications for runtime integration:
- Prioritize fusion of small pointwise ops and qkv projection to reduce kernel count. This yields immediate tail-latency wins even when algorithmic changes (e.g., Flash) are present.
- Treat FlashAttention as a compute kernel that benefits from fused inputs/outputs; avoid unnecessary copies into canonical layouts expected by Flash kernels. Where possible, adapt upstream kernels to provide Flash-friendly layouts.
- Implement async KV paging with double-buffering and overlap memcpy with compute. Page cold KV out to pinned host memory and ensure a prefetching policy driven by request heat.
- Add a gated rollout for paged KV: enable for customers/models with long-context needs and provide smoothing policies (max inflight page transfers) to bound tail latency.
- Add telemetry: kernel-launch counts, memcpy busy time, and a per-request KB of paged transfers; expose these in Redwood Console to help customers tune policies.

Open questions and next experiments:
- Quantify benefit of H100 tensor-core-specific Flash kernels vs A100 — we saw hints of better scaling on H100, need systematic runs.
- Evaluate interaction of quantized kernels (8-bit QAT/LLM.int8) with FlashAttention and fusion paths — some fused implementations currently assume FP16.
- Experiment with batching policies: is it better to coalesce short requests to amortize launch cost or to optimize single-request path? We need production traffic traces to replay.
- Investigate compiler-driven automatic fusion for common attention patterns to reduce engineering surface area for each new model variant.

Action items:
- (Aisha) Merge small-kernel fusion patch to runtime branch and run canary on staging for short-seq p99 improvements (due: 2026-03-10).
- (Liam) Prototype async paged-KV double-buffering in paged-kv-v4 branch and produce benchmark comparing overlapped vs non-overlapped transfer for 4k seq (due: 2026-03-12).
- (Priya) Run systematic H100 runs for 7B/33B with Flash+fusion vs baseline and report (due: 2026-03-09).
- (Marco) Add telemetry hooks for kernel-launch counts and memcpy busy time to Redwood Console metrics (POC dashboard by 2026-03-15).

Notes to self / messy notes:
- saw weird CUDA stream sync when using cuBLASLt + custom kernels — may be driver ordering; try isolating streams per-request.
- For seq=4096 on A100 we hit an OOM on baseline but paged-kv allowed batch=2; measured throughput improvement ~2.6x vs baseline (baseline single request only).
- Some models with rotary embeddings require embedding-specific fusion adjustments (rotation inside fused qkv).

References / links:
- flashattention v2 experiments (internal): https://github.com/redwood/inference/compare/flash-v2
- paged-kv implementation notes (doc): confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRV/Paged+KV+Design
- related PR: https://github.com/redwood/inference/pull/812

This document is a working draft — will iterate as more controlled benchmarks (esp. on H100 and quantized paths) come in.
